Newborn Care

Vaginal discharge and spotting in a newborn’s diaper

Updated: November 16, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A faint pink streak in a newborn’s diaper can be startling. A little white mucus or brief spotting can come from the vagina in the first days after birth. Notice when it appeared, how much there is and how your baby is behaving. If you cannot tell where blood came from, call your baby’s healthcare team.

Why mucus or a little blood can appear

During pregnancy, estrogen from the pregnant parent crosses the placenta. After birth the level falls. The labia, the soft folds around the vaginal opening, may look puffy. Some babies have whitish mucus. A little spotting can also appear as the uterine lining responds to the change in hormones.

The timing and amount help your clinician interpret the mark. Seattle Children’s describes normal newborn spotting as starting between the second and tenth day of life and lasting up to three or four days. This refers to light spots. Call if the amount increases, bleeding lasts longer, or it stops and comes back.

How to clean the area during a change

Wash your hands and use a clean soft cloth with warm water. Wipe from front to back, using a clean part of the cloth for each pass. If stool gets between the outer folds, gently part them just enough to clean the visible skin. Pat dry and put on a fresh diaper.

Leave the vaginal opening alone. Repeated wiping to remove every trace of mucus can irritate the skin. Keep soap, perfumed wipes and cotton swabs out of the opening. If the folds look stuck together, ask your baby’s clinician to examine them. Forcing them apart can injure the skin.

When to call about discharge or bleeding

Contact the healthcare team promptly if there is more than light spotting, an unpleasant smell, increasing redness, tenderness or swelling. Call if blood appears to come from the urine or stool or you cannot tell where it came from. A diaper saved from the change can help show the team what you saw.

A newborn with a temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher needs immediate medical assessment. Seek urgent help if your baby is difficult to wake, looks very unwell or has heavy ongoing bleeding. A change in feeding or fewer wet diapers is important information to share when you call.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Note when the mark first appeared and whether it is fading or increasing.

Use a soft cloth and water on the external skin.

Seek immediate assessment for fever in a newborn.

How BeMama can help

BeMama suggests describing what you actually saw during the change. A faint streak, repeated spots and blood that is still flowing give the clinician different information.

When to seek help

A newborn with a temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher, ongoing heavy bleeding or marked difficulty waking needs urgent medical attention.

Evidence notes updated: November 16, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Minor mucus or light spotting can follow hormone changes after birth.
  • Wipe the visible outer folds gently with warm water, working from front to back.
  • Increasing, recurring or persistent bleeding needs medical advice.

Frequently asked questions

Why is there white discharge in the diaper?

A small amount of whitish mucus can appear after hormone exposure before birth. It usually fades. Contact your clinician about a persistent or changing discharge, especially if there is an unusual smell or irritation.

Can a pink streak be normal?

A few spots can occur in the first days as hormone levels fall. More than a small amount, continued or returning bleeding, or blood of uncertain origin needs medical advice.

Should I clean inside the vaginal opening?

No. Gently clean the visible skin and the outer folds from front to back. Mucus in the opening does not need to be removed.

Why do the outer folds look swollen?

Hormonal changes can temporarily make the labia puffy. Increasing swelling, redness or tenderness or a baby who seems unwell deserves assessment.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
